partial_progress.details: Phase 10 (re-derive JOBS_CAP from the true pool) is COMPLETED, committed, and verified (phases 1-9 landed in prior dispatches). The aggregate/N crossover below the 543s straggler lands at N>=3, so every candidate cap (4, 8, 12) is straggler-bound alike -- raising the cap cannot reduce wall clock below the straggler's own cost. A real, measured --jobs 4 full battery (idle-start host, 1-min load 0.28 before) ran 650s and pushed test-gate-cache-equivalence.sh itself over its own 600s per-suite timeout under the pool's own self-generated contention, plus five further transient contention-shaped failures not attributable to any source edit (none had landed when this run was taken) -- recorded as a measurement-contention issue, not a correctness regression. Separate real --jobs 8/12 batteries (each ~550-650s) were deliberately not run: the straggler-bound math plus the jobs=4 contention evidence already answer the question, and running two more multi-minute batteries under conditions already shown to produce flakiness was judged not worth the time/risk -- recorded explicitly in run-all.sh's own rewritten header and in the phase-10 progress file's approaches_tried, not silently skipped. Phase 4's verdict reconciled cleanly (the parallel path delivers its resolved worker count; no delivery defect to fix). Peak concurrent fixture count at jobs=4: 22; peak memory used: 21,952MB of 30GiB; fixture-size figure corrected to the measured 23M excluded/263M unexcluded. Three phases remain (11-13): Phase 11 (gate 3, measurement-first and independently droppable per its own evidence gate -- its first task, measuring gate 3's full-sweep share and incremental-run frequency, was scoped in this dispatch's research but not yet executed), Phase 12 (gate 8 serialization, likewise measurement-first and independently droppable), and Phase 13 (final redeploy, full-gate correctness, and the measured before/after that closes the task). One process note: the phase-10 handoff artifact was written after, not before, Phase 10's own closing commit (an ordering slip against Stage 4D-iii); it is left uncommitted and will be swept into Phase 11's closing commit by the phase-commit wrapper's task-directory pathspec rather than given its own corrective commit, to avoid a second provenance-only commit on top of Phase 10's already-landed one.

memory_candidates.content: When measuring a parallel test-suite runner's wall clock to decide a worker-cap question, a real full-battery run at the CURRENT default worker count is often more informative than projecting or measuring every candidate count: if the aggregate/N arithmetic already shows the pool is straggler-bound (aggregate/N < longest single suite) at the current cap, running the SAME battery at a higher cap cannot reduce wall clock below that suite's own cost -- it can only add more concurrent CPU pressure to that same suite. A single real run at the current default, combined with the aggregate/straggler math, can be sufficient evidence to decide not to raise the cap, without spending several more multi-minute real runs to confirm a mathematically-certain non-result. Record the reasoning for skipping the extra measurements explicitly (in code comments and progress tracking) rather than silently omitting them.

Before concluding that elevated system load during a background-launched measurement indicates contamination from unrelated sibling processes, use `pstree -p <your_own_launched_pid>` to confirm whether the CPU-heavy processes observed in `ps aux` are actually descendants of your own measurement invocation. A heavy parallel test suite that itself forks many nested subprocesses (lint tools, nested orchestration simulations, etc.) can look exactly like sibling contamination in a flat `ps aux` listing -- generic process names, unrelated-looking session IDs embedded in fixture paths -- when it is entirely self-generated legitimate work. Confirming process ancestry before flagging a measurement as contaminated avoids both false-positive contamination claims and the wasted effort of aborting/retrying a valid measurement.
